STAT1
Descriptive statistics: center, spread
and outliers
Practice: STAT1_... sheet in C1_M08_STATISTICS_CANONICAL_PRACTICE_WORKBOOK_RC1.xlsx
1. Why this lesson matters
Business data varies. A good analyst must summarize that variation without turning a useful
statistic into a false certainty. This lesson teaches one reasoning tool and its interpretation
boundary.
2. What you are learning
Choose and interpret mean, median, percentiles, IQR, range and sample standard deviation
without reducing a dataset to one misleading number.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
No prior statistics formula is assumed.
4. Picture it in your head
Imagine describing a classroom. The mean is everyone's score averaged; the median is the
middle person; SD/IQR describe how spread out the class is. One unusual score may pull the
mean without representing the typical student.
5. New words before we use them
Mean = arithmetic average. Median = middle ordered value. Percentile = relative position.
Range = max-min. IQR = Q3-Q1. Sample SD = spread around sample mean. Outlier fence =
investigation rule, not deletion command.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED_VISUAL. StatQuest - Calculating the Mean, Variance and Standard Deviation,
Clearly Explained!!! | Full focused video. Why watch: Visual explanation of center/variance/SD
before the course adds median/IQR/outlier investigation. Internal fallback: STAT1 learner book +
workbook fully teach center/spread/outlier rules.

STAT1 - Follow with me once
7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
Mean uses every value and is sensitive to extremes. Median is resistant to extreme observations.
Standard deviation describes spread around the mean; IQR describes the middle 50%. An outlier
flag is a reason to investigate, not a deletion command. Worked example: Delivery minutes [20,
22, 24, 25, 150]. The mean is pulled upward by 150 while the median stays near the typical
routine delivery. For a highly right-skewed metric, report median plus percentiles/IQR alongside
the mean rather than claiming one number is the whole story. Guided action: Use the practice
sheet to calculate center/spread on delivery times and identify possible outliers using the 1.5 x
IQR rule.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Recompute one statistic independently, verify the row count, and explain whether any flagged
outlier is a data error, rare valid case, or unknown.
9. Why it worked
The statistic is connected to the correct population/sample/metric and units, and the
interpretation stays inside its assumptions. A second calculation, simulation, visual or quality
check provides independent evidence instead of trusting one formula cell.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Reporting only the mean for skewed data; automatically deleting an extreme value because it is
inconvenient.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
1) Restate the business question and unit. 2) Write the sample/population and metric. 3) Check
counts/data quality. 4) Recompute the simplest component. 5) Use the visual simulation for
intuition if assigned. 6) Open protected review only after saving the attempt.
STAT1 - Do alone, validate and master
12. Now you do a small version alone
Analyze a changed support-resolution dataset. Decide which center/spread summary is most
defensible and explain why.
13. Validate your result
Recompute one statistic independently, verify the row count, and explain whether any flagged
outlier is a data error, rare valid case, or unknown.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Without the book open, explain when mean vs median is more representative and why an outlier
rule does not automatically justify deletion.

STAT2
Distributions, percentiles, normal
models and z-scores
Practice: STAT2_... sheet in C1_M08_STATISTICS_CANONICAL_PRACTICE_WORKBOOK_RC1.xlsx
1. Why this lesson matters
Business data varies. A good analyst must summarize that variation without turning a useful
statistic into a false certainty. This lesson teaches one reasoning tool and its interpretation
boundary.
2. What you are learning
Read distribution shape, use percentiles and z-scores, and state when a normal model is or is not
a reasonable approximation.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
Prerequisite: STAT1 concepts plus ordinary percentage/ratio reasoning. The new statistical idea
is taught from first principles.
4. Picture it in your head
A distribution is a landscape of values. Percentiles tell where a value sits in that landscape. A
z-score measures distance from the mean in SD units only when mean/SD and model
assumptions are useful.
5. New words before we use them
Distribution = pattern/spread of values. Normal model = symmetric bell-shaped probability
model. z-score = (value-mean)/SD. P90 = 90th percentile. Skew = asymmetric tail. Unusual =
rare relative to model, not automatically erroneous.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED_VISUAL. StatQuest - The Normal Distribution, Clearly Explained!!! | Full focused
video. Why watch: See the normal model visually before deciding whether z-score/normal
language fits a business metric. Internal fallback: STAT2 learner book + workbook teach
distribution shape, percentiles and z-score limits.

STAT2 - Follow with me once
7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
A distribution shows how values are spread. Percentiles express relative position. A z-score is
(value - mean) / standard deviation. Normal models are useful only when the shape/assumptions
are a reasonable approximation. Worked example: If mean handle time is 12 minutes and SD is
3, an 18-minute call has z = +2. It is two standard deviations above the mean. That makes it
unusual relative to the model, not automatically invalid. Guided action: Compare a
near-symmetric service-time sample with a skewed purchase-value sample. Compute selected
percentiles and z-scores.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Check shape visually and compare mean/median before using normal-model language.
9. Why it worked
The statistic is connected to the correct population/sample/metric and units, and the
interpretation stays inside its assumptions. A second calculation, simulation, visual or quality
check provides independent evidence instead of trusting one formula cell.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Assuming every business metric is normal; calling a high z-score automatically wrong.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
1) Restate the business question and unit. 2) Write the sample/population and metric. 3) Check
counts/data quality. 4) Recompute the simplest component. 5) Use the visual simulation for
intuition if assigned. 6) Open protected review only after saving the attempt.

STAT3
Population, samples and sampling
bias
Practice: STAT3_... sheet in C1_M08_STATISTICS_CANONICAL_PRACTICE_WORKBOOK_RC1.xlsx
1. Why this lesson matters
Business data varies. A good analyst must summarize that variation without turning a useful
statistic into a false certainty. This lesson teaches one reasoning tool and its interpretation
boundary.
2. What you are learning
Define the target population, sample, sampling frame and main bias risks before generalizing.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
Prerequisite: STAT2 concepts plus ordinary percentage/ratio reasoning. The new statistical idea
is taught from first principles.
4. Picture it in your head
Population is everyone you want to talk about; sampling frame is the actual list you can reach;
sample is who you observed. If the frame misses a group, more responses from the same frame
do not magically include them.
5. New words before we use them
Target population = group you want to infer about. Sample = observed units. Sampling frame =
units eligible to be selected. Sampling error = chance sample variation. Sampling bias =
systematic selection distortion. Nonresponse = selected units do not respond.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED_VISUAL. StatQuest - Sampling from a Distribution, Clearly Explained!!! | Full
focused video. Why watch: Makes random sampling variation visible before the course
distinguishes chance error from systematic sampling bias. Internal fallback: STAT3 learner book
+ sampling-design sheet fully teach population/frame/bias/generalization.

STAT3 - Follow with me once
7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
Random sampling error is chance variation between samples. Sampling bias is systematic and
does not disappear just because the sample is large. Selection, nonresponse and survivorship
can distort conclusions. Worked example: A survey sent only to recent support users can
overrepresent frustrated customers. Ten thousand such responses can be less representative
than a smaller probability sample of all active customers. Guided action: Classify four sampling
designs by population, frame, likely bias and repair.
8. What you should see / be able to say
State who could never be selected under your design and whether that limits the target
population.
9. Why it worked
The statistic is connected to the correct population/sample/metric and units, and the
interpretation stays inside its assumptions. A second calculation, simulation, visual or quality
check provides independent evidence instead of trusting one formula cell.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Generalizing beyond the sampled population; believing sample size repairs selection bias.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
1) Restate the business question and unit. 2) Write the sample/population and metric. 3) Check
counts/data quality. 4) Recompute the simplest component. 5) Use the visual simulation for
intuition if assigned. 6) Open protected review only after saving the attempt.

STAT4
Sampling distributions, standard
error and the CLT
Practice: STAT4_... sheet in C1_M08_STATISTICS_CANONICAL_PRACTICE_WORKBOOK_RC1.xlsx
1. Why this lesson matters
Business data varies. A good analyst must summarize that variation without turning a useful
statistic into a false certainty. This lesson teaches one reasoning tool and its interpretation
boundary.
2. What you are learning
Explain why estimates vary from sample to sample and how sample size affects standard error
and precision.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
Prerequisite: STAT3 concepts plus ordinary percentage/ratio reasoning. The new statistical idea
is taught from first principles.
4. Picture it in your head
Take many samples from the same population. Each sample mean moves a little. Those sample
means form their own distribution. SE describes that estimator movement; it usually shrinks as n
grows.
5. New words before we use them
Statistic = number calculated from sample. Sampling distribution = distribution of a statistic
across repeated samples. Standard error (SE) = SD of estimator/sampling distribution. CLT =
sample means often approach normal under broad conditions as n grows.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED_VISUAL. StatQuest - The Central Limit Theorem, Clearly Explained!!! | Full
focused video. Why watch: Visualize repeated sample means and why their spread changes with
n. Internal fallback: STAT4 learner book + visual simulation notebook teach SD vs SE and CLT.

STAT4 - Follow with me once
7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
A statistic such as a sample mean varies across repeated samples. Standard error describes
variability of an estimator. For a mean, SE is commonly approximated by sample SD / sqrt(n).
The CLT explains why sample means often become approximately normal under broad
conditions as n grows. Worked example: If two surveys have the same SD but one has 9 times as
many observations, its standard error is roughly one-third as large because sqrt(9)=3. More
precision does not repair a biased sample. Guided action: Use the workbook and simulation
notebook to compare repeated sample means for n=10, 40 and 160.
8. What you should see / be able to say
Check that the observed spread of repeated sample means decreases with n while the
underlying population spread stays similar.
9. Why it worked
The statistic is connected to the correct population/sample/metric and units, and the
interpretation stays inside its assumptions. A second calculation, simulation, visual or quality
check provides independent evidence instead of trusting one formula cell.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Confusing SD with SE; confusing precision with representativeness.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
1) Restate the business question and unit. 2) Write the sample/population and metric. 3) Check
counts/data quality. 4) Recompute the simplest component. 5) Use the visual simulation for
intuition if assigned. 6) Open protected review only after saving the attempt.
STAT4 - Do alone, validate and master
12. Now you do a small version alone
Explain how a changed sample-size decision affects precision without claiming it fixes bias.
13. Validate your result
Check that the observed spread of repeated sample means decreases with n while the
underlying population spread stays similar.
14. Teach it back in your own words
Explain SD vs SE and why CLT is about the sampling distribution, not magically normalizing the
raw data.

STAT5
Confidence intervals and uncertainty
Practice: STAT5_... sheet in C1_M08_STATISTICS_CANONICAL_PRACTICE_WORKBOOK_RC1.xlsx
1. Why this lesson matters
Business data varies. A good analyst must summarize that variation without turning a useful
statistic into a false certainty. This lesson teaches one reasoning tool and its interpretation
boundary.
2. What you are learning
Compute and interpret approximate confidence intervals while separating precision from bias.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
Prerequisite: STAT4 concepts plus ordinary percentage/ratio reasoning. The new statistical idea
is taught from first principles.
4. Picture it in your head
A confidence interval is a ruler around an estimate built by a repeated procedure. A narrower
ruler means more precision under assumptions; it cannot reveal selection bias by itself.
5. New words before we use them
Point estimate = one estimated value. Confidence interval (CI) = interval from a procedure.
Confidence level = long-run capture rate under assumptions. Precision = interval narrowness.
Bias = systematic shift from target; narrow does not imply unbiased.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED_VISUAL. StatQuest - Confidence Intervals, Clearly Explained!!! | Full focused
video. Why watch: Visual CI intuition before the course focuses on repeated-procedure
interpretation, precision and bias. Internal fallback: STAT5 learner book + workbook + simulation
notebook fully teach the CI interpretation contract.
Open visual source
STAT5 - Follow with me once
7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
A 95% confidence procedure is designed to capture the true parameter in about 95% of repeated
samples under its assumptions. A narrower interval means greater precision, not automatically
less bias. Always report the estimate itself. Worked example: Estimated conversion lift +0.5
percentage points with 95% CI [-0.2pp, +1.2pp] does not exclude zero at the 95% level. Positive
business-relevant effects may still be plausible. Guided action: Calculate approximate mean CIs
for n=100 and n=900 with the same mean and SD.

STAT6
Hypothesis testing, null hypothesis
and p-values
Practice: STAT6_... sheet in C1_M08_STATISTICS_CANONICAL_PRACTICE_WORKBOOK_RC1.xlsx
1. Why this lesson matters
Business data varies. A good analyst must summarize that variation without turning a useful
statistic into a false certainty. This lesson teaches one reasoning tool and its interpretation
boundary.
2. What you are learning
Interpret a p-value under a pre-declared decision rule without treating it as a truth probability.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
Prerequisite: STAT5 concepts plus ordinary percentage/ratio reasoning. The new statistical idea
is taught from first principles.
4. Picture it in your head
Start with a baseline/no-effect story H0. Ask: if that story were true, how surprising would data
this extreme be? The p-value answers that conditional question—not the probability that H0 itself
is true.
5. New words before we use them
Null hypothesis H0 = baseline/no-effect model. Alternative = competing effect model. Alpha =
predeclared significance cutoff. p-value = tail probability of data this/extremer under H0.
Reject/fail to reject = decision language, not truth proof.
6. Watch / visual source
RECOMMENDED_VISUAL. StatQuest - Hypothesis Testing and The Null Hypothesis, Clearly
Explained!!! | 0:22-13:44. Why watch: See null/reject/fail-to-reject logic before applying the
analyst decision rule. Internal fallback: STAT6 learner book + workbook teach two-proportion test
and safe p-value language. Optional companion: StatQuest - p-values: What they are and how to
interpret them | 0:17-9:47.

STAT6 - Follow with me once
7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
The null hypothesis is the baseline/no-effect model. A p-value asks how surprising the observed
data or more extreme data would be if the null were true. p < alpha is statistically significant
under that rule; failing to reject H0 is not proving H0. Worked example: If p=0.08 at alpha=0.05,
write: the data do not provide enough evidence to reject the null at 0.05. Do not write: there is
no effect. Guided action: Use the practice A/B summary to compute/interpret a two-proportion
z-test at analyst depth.
8. What you should see / be able to say
State the null, alpha, estimate, p-value and decision separately.
9. Why it worked
The statistic is connected to the correct population/sample/metric and units, and the
interpretation stays inside its assumptions. A second calculation, simulation, visual or quality
check provides independent evidence instead of trusting one formula cell.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Saying p=0.03 means a 3% probability the null is true; saying p>0.05 proves no effect.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
1) Restate the business question and unit. 2) Write the sample/population and metric. 3) Check
counts/data quality. 4) Recompute the simplest component. 5) Use the visual simulation for
intuition if assigned. 6) Open protected review only after saving the attempt.

STAT7
Effect size, practical significance and
decision thresholds
Practice: STAT7_... sheet in C1_M08_STATISTICS_CANONICAL_PRACTICE_WORKBOOK_RC1.xlsx
1. Why this lesson matters
Business data varies. A good analyst must summarize that variation without turning a useful
statistic into a false certainty. This lesson teaches one reasoning tool and its interpretation
boundary.
2. What you are learning
Separate evidence of a difference from whether the difference is large enough to matter.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
Prerequisite: STAT6 concepts plus ordinary percentage/ratio reasoning. The new statistical idea
is taught from first principles.
4. Picture it in your head
Statistical evidence asks whether a difference is distinguishable from chance under assumptions.
Business significance asks whether the size is worth money/risk/effort. These are separate
decision axes.
5. New words before we use them
Absolute lift = treatment-control in percentage points. Relative lift = absolute lift/control.
Minimum worthwhile effect = business threshold. Guardrail = metric not allowed to worsen
beyond limit. Practical significance = effect matters operationally/economically.
6. Watch / visual source
OPTIONAL_VISUAL_COMPANION. StatQuest - p-values: What they are and how to interpret them |
Ending emphasis: p-values do not measure effect size. Why watch: Useful bridge from
significance to effect size/business thresholds. Internal fallback: STAT7 learner book + workbook
are the canonical teacher.

STAT7 - Follow with me once
7. Follow with me once - fully worked teacher demonstration
Absolute lift = treatment rate - control rate. Relative lift = absolute lift / control rate. Tiny effects
can be statistically significant in huge samples; valuable effects can be uncertain in small
samples. Define a minimum worthwhile effect and guardrails before seeing results when
possible. Worked example: Control conversion 5.0%, treatment 5.4%: absolute lift +0.4
percentage points; relative lift 8%. Whether +0.4pp matters depends on economics, risk and
costs. Guided action: Calculate absolute/relative lift and compare it with a stated minimum
worthwhile effect and a guardrail threshold.
8. What you should see / be able to say
State estimate, uncertainty, business threshold and guardrail separately.
9. Why it worked
The statistic is connected to the correct population/sample/metric and units, and the
interpretation stays inside its assumptions. A second calculation, simulation, visual or quality
check provides independent evidence instead of trusting one formula cell.
10. Common beginner mistakes
Calling every statistically significant result important; ignoring a damaged guardrail metric.
11. If you get stuck - recovery ladder
1) Restate the business question and unit. 2) Write the sample/population and metric. 3) Check
counts/data quality. 4) Recompute the simplest component. 5) Use the visual simulation for
intuition if assigned. 6) Open protected review only after saving the attempt.

STAT8
Correlation, confounding and causal
claims
Practice: STAT8_... sheet in C1_M08_STATISTICS_CANONICAL_PRACTICE_WORKBOOK_RC1.xlsx
1. Why this lesson matters
Business data varies. A good analyst must summarize that variation without turning a useful
statistic into a false certainty. This lesson teaches one reasoning tool and its interpretation
boundary.
2. What you are learning
Quantify linear association while respecting the limits of observational evidence.
3. What you already need / prerequisite
Prerequisite: STAT7 concepts plus ordinary percentage/ratio reasoning. The new statistical idea
is taught from first principles.
4. Picture it in your head
Two lines can move together because X causes Y, Y causes X, or Z moves both. Correlation
measures linear association; the causal story needs stronger design/evidence.

WORKED PATTERN STAT9 - Follow with me once Define treatment/control and unit of

support contacts? Guided action: Audit an A/B-test plan, then analyze the integrated experiment
dataset. Before using Experiment_Data, use a tiny thought experiment: control 100/1000 = 10%;
treatment 110/1000 = 11%. Absolute lift = +1pp; relative lift = +10%. If minimum worthwhile

uncertainty. This separates 'effect exists?' from 'large enough to matter?'.

Important distinction: "point estimate exceeds MWE" and "the uncertainty interval establishes at least the MWE" are different
claims. M08 should never collapse them into one boolean.
Expected decision language
Under the canonical RC1 rule, LAUNCH / progress is acceptable subject to implementation checks. RC2 qualification: the
observed +3.0pp clears the 1.0pp threshold, but the 95% CI lower bound does not establish an effect of at least 1.0pp. Do not
describe the full MWE as statistically guaranteed.
Critical interpretation checks
• State the null hypothesis and alpha separately from the estimated effect.
• Use p-value language conditional on H0; never write that p is the probability H0 is true.
• Use percentage points for absolute rate differences and percent for relative lift.
• Treat the 95% CI as uncertainty around the effect estimate; do not claim a fixed parameter has a 95% posterior probability
unless a Bayesian model was actually used.
• A statistically significant result is not automatically business-important. A business-important point estimate is not
automatically statistically established.
• Guardrails can block rollout even when the primary metric improves.
Layer 4 - Diagnostic decision tree
• Counts/labels wrong: stop. Repair data integrity before calculating rates.
• Rates wrong: check numerator/denominator and whether percentages use the full assigned group.
• pp vs % wrong: absolute lift = Treatment% - Control%; relative lift = absolute lift / Control%.
• z/p wrong: verify pooled SE for the null test and a two-sided p-value.
• CI wrong: verify the unpooled SE for the rate difference and keep units in percentage points.
• Decision too strong: separately evaluate design/data quality, effect estimate, uncertainty/statistical evidence, MWE and
guardrail.
• Conclusion copied from review: no pass. Close review and complete changed fresh evidence.

Important distinction: "point estimate exceeds MWE" and "the uncertainty interval establishes at least the MWE" are different
claims. M08 should never collapse them into one boolean.
Expected decision language
DO NOT CLAIM A WIN. The point estimate does not clear the 1.0pp minimum worthwhile effect, the CI spans negative and
positive effects, and p is far above 0.05. Guardrail is fine, but that alone is not evidence of primary-metric value.
Critical interpretation checks
• State the null hypothesis and alpha separately from the estimated effect.
• Use p-value language conditional on H0; never write that p is the probability H0 is true.
• Use percentage points for absolute rate differences and percent for relative lift.
• Treat the 95% CI as uncertainty around the effect estimate; do not claim a fixed parameter has a 95% posterior probability
unless a Bayesian model was actually used.
• A statistically significant result is not automatically business-important. A business-important point estimate is not
automatically statistically established.
• Guardrails can block rollout even when the primary metric improves.
Layer 4 - Diagnostic decision tree
• Counts/labels wrong: stop. Repair data integrity before calculating rates.
• Rates wrong: check numerator/denominator and whether percentages use the full assigned group.
• pp vs % wrong: absolute lift = Treatment% - Control%; relative lift = absolute lift / Control%.
• z/p wrong: verify pooled SE for the null test and a two-sided p-value.
• CI wrong: verify the unpooled SE for the rate difference and keep units in percentage points.
• Decision too strong: separately evaluate design/data quality, effect estimate, uncertainty/statistical evidence, MWE and
guardrail.
• Conclusion copied from review: no pass. Close review and complete changed fresh evidence.
